--- title: "K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # Clustering

Lecture A: K-means clustering (dissimilarity, within-cluster variation, algorithm)

Lecture B: Hierarchical clustering (linkages, dendrograms) and choosing the number of clusters

::: notes - Slides adapted from Ryan Tibshirani's Data Mining class notes. All figures are regenerated with simulated data so they are reproducible. - R scripts: kmeans-exmp.R, hclust-exmp.R, more-on-linkage.R, kclust.R in the course code repository. ::: # Lecture A: K-Means Clustering {#part-a} ## Don't Confuse Clustering and Classification! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Classification (supervised)** - Data whose groups are **known** - Learn what differentiates the groups (a classification function) to classify future data - e.g. handwritten digits 0-9 with labels ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Clustering (unsupervised)** - Groups are **unknown and undefined** - Learn the groups themselves, as well as what differentiates them ::: :::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Dissimilarity and Within-Cluster Scatter - Observations $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and **dissimilarities** $d(X_i,X_j)$, e.g. $X_i\in\R^p$ and $d(X_i,X_j) = \|X_i - X_j\|_2^2$. - A **clustering** $C$ assigns each $X_i$ to a group $C(i) = k\in\{1,\dots,K\}$; $n_k$ points in group $k$; $d_{ij} = d(X_i,X_j)$. The **within-cluster scatter** is $$ W = \frac12\sum_{k=1}^K\frac1{n_k}\sum_{C(i)=k,\,C(j)=k} d_{ij}. $$ Smaller $W$ is better. ## Simple Example: $n = 5$, $K = 2$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} P <- rbind(c(0.70, 0.02), c(0.95, 0.40), c(0.02, 0.70), c(0.38, 0.55), c(0.43, 0.97)) D <- as.matrix(dist(P))^2 round(D, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 4 5 1 0.00 0.21 0.92 0.38 0.98 2 0.21 0.00 0.95 0.35 0.60 3 0.92 0.95 0.00 0.15 0.24 4 0.38 0.35 0.15 0.00 0.18 5 0.98 0.60 0.24 0.18 0.00 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} W <- function(cl, D) sum(sapply(unique(cl), function(k) sum(D[cl == k, cl == k]) / sum(cl == k))) / 2 c(red = W(c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2), D), blue = W(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2), D)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` red blue 0.4330 0.2941 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip The `dist()` function computes all pairwise distances (Euclidean by default; see `method =`). ::: ## Finding the Best Group Assignments Why not search over all clusterings $C$? The number of possible assignments of $n$ points into $K$ nonempty groups is $$ A(n,K) = \frac1{K!}\sum_{k=1}^K(-1)^{K-k}\binom Kk k^n . $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} A <- function(n, K) sum((-1)^(K - (1:K)) * choose(K, 1:K) * (1:K)^n) / factorial(K) c(A(10, 4), A(25, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.410e+04 4.677e+13 ``` ::: ::: - $A(10,4) = 34{,}105$ and $A(25,4)\approx 5\times10^{13}$: hopeless for realistic $n$. We settle for an **approximation**. ## Rewriting the Within-Cluster Scatter For Euclidean data and $d_{ij} = \|X_i - X_j\|_2^2$: $$ \frac12\sum_{k=1}^K\frac1{n_k}\sum_{C(i)=k}\sum_{C(j)=k}\|X_i-X_j\|_2^2 = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i-\bar X_k\|_2^2, $$ where $\bar X_k = \frac1{n_k}\sum_{C(i)=k}X_i$. The right-hand side is the **within-cluster variation**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cl <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2) c(scatter = W(cl, D), wcv = sum(sapply(1:2, function(k) sum(sweep(P[cl == k, , drop = FALSE], 2, colMeans(P[cl == k, , drop = FALSE]))^2)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` scatter wcv 0.2941 0.2941 ``` ::: ::: ## Rewriting the Minimization - For any $Z_1,\dots,Z_m$, $\sum_i\|Z_i - c\|_2^2$ is minimized by $c = \bar Z$. - So minimizing the within-cluster variation is the same as minimizing the **enlarged criterion** $$ \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i - c_k\|_2^2 \quad\text{over both } C \text{ and } c_1,\dots,c_K\in\R^p. $$ ## The K-Means Algorithm ::: algo Start with an initial guess for $c_1,\dots,c_K$ (e.g. $K$ random points). Repeat: 1. **Minimize over $C$:** for each $i$, find the closest center $c_k$ to $X_i$ and let $C(i) = k$. 2. **Minimize over $c_1,\dots,c_K$:** for each $k$, let $c_k = \bar X_k$, the average of points in group $k$. Stop when the within-cluster variation does not change. ::: In words: (1) label each point by its closest center; (2) replace each center by the average of its points. ## K-Means from Scratch ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} my_kmeans <- function(X, K, centers = X[sample(nrow(X), K), , drop = FALSE], maxit = 50) { history <- list(centers) for (it in 1:maxit) { d <- sapply(1:K, function(k) colSums((t(X) - centers[k, ])^2)) # n x K squared distances cl <- max.col(-d) # step 1: closest center new <- t(sapply(1:K, function(k) colMeans(X[cl == k, , drop = FALSE]))) # step 2: averages history[[it + 1]] <- new if (all(abs(new - centers) < 1e-10)) break centers <- new } wcv <- sum(sapply(1:K, function(k) sum(sweep(X[cl == k, , drop = FALSE], 2, centers[k, ])^2))) list(cluster = cl, centers = centers, wcv = wcv, iter = it, history = history) } ``` ::: ## K-Means Example: $n = 300$, $K = 3$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) X300 <- make_blobs(300, rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 1.4), c(1.2, 0.6)), sd = 0.22) init <- rbind(c(1.2, 1.3), c(0.2, -0.3), c(0.3, 0.2)) fit <- my_kmeans(X300, 3, centers = init) par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1)) cols <- c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60") for (it in c(1, 2, 3, length(fit$history))) { cen <- fit$history[[it]] cl <- max.col(-sapply(1:3, function(k) colSums((t(X300) - cen[k, ])^2))) plot(X300, col = if (it == 1) "gray60" else adjustcolor(cols[cl], .4), pch = 20, main = if (it == 1) "Initial centers" else paste("Iteration", it - 1)) points(cen, pch = 19, cex = 2.5, col = cols) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Properties of K-Means - Within-cluster variation **decreases** with each iteration: if $W_t$ is the value at iteration $t$, then $W_{t+1}\le W_t$. - The algorithm **always converges**, no matter the initial centers. (In at most $K^n$ iterations. Why?) - The final clustering **depends on the initial centers**. Run K-means multiple times (e.g. 10 random starts) and keep the solution with the smallest within-cluster variation. - K-means is **not guaranteed** to find the global minimizer (that would require all $A(n,K)$ assignments!). ## Multiple Runs: $n = 250$, $K = 4$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(11) par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1)) cols4 <- c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60", "#C2185B") for (r in 1:3) { f <- my_kmeans(X250, 4) plot(X250, col = adjustcolor(cols4[f$cluster], .5), pch = 20, main = sprintf("WCV = %.1f", f$wcv)) points(f$centers, pch = 19, cex = 2.5, col = cols4) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - In R, `kmeans(X, centers = K, nstart = 20)` does this automatically (Hartigan-Wong algorithm by default). ## `kmeans()` in R and Standardization ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} km <- kmeans(X250, centers = 4, nstart = 20) km$tot.withinss; km$size ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 13.57 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 61 65 65 59 ``` ::: ::: ::: alert K-means uses Euclidean distance: variables on larger scales dominate. Usually `scale()` the variables first. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) table(kmeans(scale(iris[, 1:4]), 3, nstart = 20)$cluster, iris$Species) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` setosa versicolor virginica 1 0 39 14 2 0 11 36 3 50 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ## K-Medoids (PAM) - K-means centers are averages (not data points) and are sensitive to outliers. - **K-medoids** restricts the centers to be data points (medoids) and works with **any** dissimilarity. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(cluster) pm <- pam(X250, k = 4) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1)) plot(X250, col = adjustcolor(cols4[pm$clustering], .5), pch = 20, main = "PAM (K-medoids)") points(pm$medoids, pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 4) plot(X250, col = adjustcolor(cols4[km$cluster], .5), pch = 20, main = "K-means") points(km$centers, pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: # Lecture B: Hierarchical Clustering {#part-b} ## From K-Means to Hierarchical Clustering Recall two properties of K-means (K-medoids): 1. It fits exactly $K$ clusters (as specified). 2. The final assignment depends on the chosen initial centers. Given pairwise dissimilarities $d_{ij}$, **hierarchical clustering** produces a consistent result without choosing initial positions or the number of clusters. - The catch: we must choose a way to measure dissimilarity between **groups**, called the **linkage**. - The result is a sequence of clusterings: at one end all points are in their own cluster, at the other end all points are in one cluster. ## Agglomerative vs. Divisive :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Agglomerative** (bottom-up) - Start with all points in their own group - Until there is only one cluster, repeatedly merge the two groups with the smallest dissimilarity ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Divisive** (top-down) - Start with all points in one cluster - Until all points are in their own cluster, repeatedly split the group into two, resulting in the biggest dissimilarity ::: :::: Agglomerative strategies are simpler; we focus on them (`hclust()`). Divisive: `cluster::diana()`. ## Simple Example and the Dendrogram ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} P7 <- rbind(c(.88, .92), c(.27, .66), c(.38, .63), c(.57, .1), c(.89, .3), c(.2, .2), c(.88, .7)) hc7 <- hclust(dist(P7), method = "complete") hc7$merge # the merge sequence (negative = singletons) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] -2 -3 [2,] -1 -7 [3,] -4 -5 [4,] -6 1 [5,] 3 4 [6,] 2 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(P7, pch = 1, cex = 2, xlab = "Dimension 1", ylab = "Dimension 2", xlim = c(.1, 1)); text(P7, labels = 1:7, pos = 2) plot(hc7, main = "Dendrogram", xlab = "", sub = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## What's a Dendrogram? A tree that displays the hierarchical sequence of clusterings: - Each node represents a group; each leaf is a singleton; the root contains the whole data set. - Each internal node has two daughters: the groups that were merged to form it. - With leaves at height zero, each internal node is drawn at a height **proportional to the dissimilarity** between its two daughters. - **Cutting** the dendrogram horizontally partitions the data into clusters: `cutree(hc, h = )` or `cutree(hc, k = )`. ## Linkages - Points $X_1,\dots,X_n$, dissimilarities $d_{ij}$ (here $d_{ij} = \|X_i - X_j\|_2$, distance not squared). - Groups $G, H\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$. A **linkage** is a function $d(G,H)$ returning a dissimilarity score between groups. ::: algo Agglomerative clustering: start with all points in their own group; until there is only one cluster, merge the two groups $G, H$ with the smallest $d(G,H)$. ::: ## Single Linkage Nearest-neighbor linkage: the smallest dissimilarity between two points in opposite groups, $$ d_{\text{single}}(G,H) = \min_{i\in G,\,j\in H}d_{ij}. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: **Cut interpretation:** for each point $X_i$, there is another point $X_j$ in its cluster with $d_{ij}\le 0.9$. ## Complete Linkage Furthest-neighbor linkage: the largest dissimilarity between two points in opposite groups, $$ d_{\text{complete}}(G,H) = \max_{i\in G,\,j\in H}d_{ij}. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: **Cut interpretation:** for each point $X_i$, every other point $X_j$ in its cluster satisfies $d_{ij}\le 5$. ## Average Linkage The average dissimilarity over all pairs in opposite groups, $$ d_{\text{average}}(G,H) = \frac1{n_G\cdot n_H}\sum_{i\in G,\,j\in H}d_{ij}. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: **Cut interpretation:** there really isn't a good one! ## Shortcomings of Single, Complete, and Average Linkage - **Single** linkage suffers from **chaining**: to merge two groups, only one pair of points needs to be close. Clusters can be too spread out, not compact enough. - **Complete** linkage avoids chaining but suffers from **crowding**: a point can be closer to points in other clusters than to points in its own cluster. - **Average** linkage strikes a balance (relatively compact and relatively far apart), **but** + it is not clear what properties the clusters have when we cut the tree, and + results can change with a **monotone increasing transformation** of the $d_{ij}$ (single and complete are unchanged). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1)) for (pw in 1:2) plot(X60, col = c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60")[cutree(hclust(d60^pw, "average"), k = 3)], pch = 1, lwd = 2, main = c("Avg linkage: distance", "Avg linkage: distance^2")[pw]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Centroid Linkage Commonly used in biology (Eisen et al., 1998). With group averages $\bar X_G$, $\bar X_H$: $$ d_{\text{centroid}}(G,H) = \|\bar X_G - \bar X_H\|_2. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hc_c <- hclust(d60^2, method = "centroid") # R's centroid method expects squared distances sum(diff(hc_c$height) < 0) # number of inversions in the merge heights ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(mar = c(1, 4, 1, 1)); plot(hc_c, labels = FALSE, main = "", xlab = "", sub = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Simple, **but** can produce dendrograms with **inversions** (a merge lower than the previous one), there is no cut interpretation, and answers change under monotone transformations. ## Minimax Linkage Define the radius of a group around $X_i$ as $r(X_i, G) = \max_{j\in G}d_{ij}$. Then $$ d_{\text{minimax}}(G,H) = \min_{i\in G\cup H}r(X_i, G\cup H), $$ the smallest radius encompassing all points in $G$ and $H$; the minimizer $X_c$ is the **prototype** (Bien and Tibshirani, 2011). - **Cut interpretation:** each point is within $h$ of the center (a data point!) of its cluster. - No inversions; unchanged by monotone transformations; the hierarchical analogue of K-medoids. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hc_mm <- protoclust::protoclust(d60) plot(hc_mm, labels = FALSE, main = "Minimax linkage (protoclust)", xlab = "", sub = "") ``` ::: ## Linkage Summary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Linkage |No inversions? |Unchanged under monotone transf.? |Cut interpretation? |Notes | |:--------|:--------------|:---------------------------------|:-------------------|:-----------------------| |Single | | | |chaining | |Complete | | | |crowding | |Average | | | | | |Centroid | | | |simple | |Minimax | | | |centers are data points | ::: ::: - This doesn't tell us the "best" linkage; that is very **situation dependent**. Also: Ward's method (`method = "ward.D2"`) merges the pair that least increases the within-cluster variation. # How Many Clusters? ## This Is a Hard Problem - Sometimes $K$ is known ahead of time (segment customers for $K$ salespeople; vector quantization with $K$ codewords). - Other times $K$ is implicitly defined by cutting a tree at a given height. - In most exploratory applications $K$ is **unknown**. What is the "right" value of $K$? Why is it hard? It is hard for humans to *perform* (unless the data are low-dimensional) and just as hard to *explain* what we are looking for. Why is it important? E.g., $K=2$ vs. $K=3$ subtypes of breast cancer is a big scientific difference. ## Within-Cluster Variation Just Keeps Decreasing $$ W(K) = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i - \bar X_k\|_2^2 $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) fits <- lapply(1:10, function(k) kmeans(X250, k, nstart = 20)) Wk <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "tot.withinss"); Bk <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "betweenss") par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(X250, pch = 20, col = "gray50"); points(fits[[4]]$centers, pch = 19, cex = 2.5, col = cols4) plot(1:10, Wk, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "Within-cluster variation") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Between-Cluster Variation $$ B(K) = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k\|\bar X_k - \bar X\|_2^2,\qquad \bar X = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i $$ - Bigger $B$ is better, but $B(K)$ just keeps **increasing** with $K$. - Note $W(K) + B(K) = \text{TSS}$, constant! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(1:10, Bk, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "Between-cluster variation") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## The CH Index (Calinski and Harabasz, 1974) We want **simultaneously** a small $W$ and a large $B$: $$ \text{CH}(K) = \frac{B(K)/(K-1)}{W(K)/(n-K)},\qquad \hat K = \argmax_{K\in\{2,\dots,K_{\max}\}}\text{CH}(K). $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- nrow(X250); K <- 2:10 CH <- (Bk[K] / (K - 1)) / (Wk[K] / (n - K)) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(X250, pch = 20, col = adjustcolor(cols4[fits[[4]]$cluster], .5)) plot(K, CH, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "CH index"); abline(v = K[which.max(CH)], lty = 2, col = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - We would choose $K = 4$. **Problem:** CH is not defined for $K = 1$, so it can never choose "no clusters". ## Two More Criteria: Silhouette and Gap Statistic ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sil <- sapply(2:10, function(k) mean(silhouette(fits[[k]]$cluster, dist(X250))[, "sil_width"])) set.seed(4750) gap <- clusGap(X250, FUNcluster = kmeans, K.max = 10, B = 50, nstart = 10) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(2:10, sil, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "average silhouette width") plot(gap, main = "Gap statistic") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/07-clustering/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} maxSE(gap$Tab[, "gap"], gap$Tab[, "SE.sim"], method = "firstSEmax") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - The gap statistic (Tibshirani, Walther, Hastie 2001) compares log W(K) with its expectation under a reference (uniform) distribution, and *can* choose K = 1. ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - **K-means:** minimize within-cluster variation by alternating assignments and averages; use many random starts and standardize variables. - **K-medoids (PAM):** centers are data points; any dissimilarity. - **Hierarchical:** one tree, many clusterings; the **linkage** matters (single, complete, average, centroid, minimax, Ward). - **Choosing $K$:** elbow of $W(K)$, CH index, silhouette, gap statistic. No universal answer. ::: ::: your-turn Apply K-means and hierarchical clustering (complete and average linkage) to `scale(USArrests)`. Do the methods agree for $K = 4$? :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
